Michelle,

Thanks for your prompt response.

I'd like to request an internal review of the handling of my enquiry and,
insofar as it constitutes a Freedom of Information request, of the
conclusion that no relevant records are held.

I am not challenging the conclusion simply because it is inconvenient to my
enquiry. Rather, I would like to establish whether an adequate search was
undertaken before the conclusion was reached.

Your latest response states that the Medical Examiner Service would not
hold “any records whatsoever” or have “any knowledge” of these patients.
Given that the deaths occurred in 1983 and 1990, before the establishment
of the current Medical Examiner Service, I would be grateful if the
internal review could specifically establish whether the search extended
beyond current Medical Examiner records to any relevant predecessor, legacy
or transferred records.

In particular, could the review please confirm:

   1.

   What records and information systems were searched;
   2.

   Whether any legacy or predecessor records relating to the medical
   examination or certification of deaths were considered;
   3.

   Whether records relating to Llandough Hospital, where William Buckler is
   recorded as having died in approximately May 1990, are held by the Medical
   Examiner Service, NHS Wales Shared Services Partnership, another NHS body,
   or an archive to which you have access or knowledge;
   4.

   Whether any records concerning referrals to a coroner, inquests,
   post-mortems or other investigations into these deaths would have been held
   separately from Medical Examiner records;
   5.

   Whether the possibility of records having been transferred to an archive
   or successor organisation was considered;
   6.

   Whether the statement that no records are held means that no relevant
   records are held by the South Wales Central Medical Examiner Service
   specifically, or that searches have established that no such records are
   held anywhere within NHS Wales Shared Services Partnership; and
   7.

   If the records are not held by your organisation, whether you can
   identify the appropriate current custodian or archive for any surviving
   historical records.

For clarity, the individuals concerned are:

   - William (Billy) Buckler – died at Llandough Hospital on or about 29
   May 1990, aged 41; and
   - Mary Doreen Williams – born 10 August 1913; death registered in March
   1983, South Glamorgan, Vol. 28, p. 3029.

I would be grateful if this could be treated as a formal internal review
rather than simply a further general enquiry.

I would also ask that the review be undertaken by someone who was not
responsible for the original response, where practicable.

My purpose is to establish a reliable documentary record and, in
particular, to distinguish between:

(a) records which do not exist;

(b) records which once existed but have been destroyed;

(c) records which exist but are held by another organisation; and

(d) records which are held within NHS Wales or a predecessor organisation
but were not identified by the original search.

I would be grateful for confirmation of the review and, where applicable,
the relevant FOI reference number.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergeant)

Royal Signals Cyber and Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Good morning, Mr Buckler
Thank you for your e-mail dated 20/08/2026.

Although appointed and paid for by local councils, the coroner is not a local government officer but holds office under the Crown.

Coroners are not designated as public authorities under the Freedom of Information Act 2000 and therefore their records are not subject to the information access regime of this Act.

Please let me know if I can be of further assistance.
Kind Regards
Bev Morgan

Thank you for your enquiry of 13/08/2026 regarding a review of:



We are handling your request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.



From our initial assessment it is clear that we will not be able to answer your request without further clarification. Under section 1(3) of the Act, a public authority need not comply with a request unless any further information reasonably required to locate the information is supplied.



In order to progress your request, we require clarification on the scope of your request.



The FOI Centre has received a request for the following:



My request was deliberately framed more broadly than a simple catalogue search for the words “Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or “Cedfin”. I specifically asked The National Archives to identify recorded information concerning the existence, transfer, retention, destruction, disposal or absence of records, including records that might not be catalogued under the property's later or local names.



Your response confirms only that you searched the PRO and RW series using:



“Great House Farm” OR “Ty Mawr” OR Llandough OR Cedfin



combined with “Glamorgan”, and that this produced no catalogue results.



You also correctly state that Discovery searches catalogue titles and descriptions rather than the contents of records. That qualification is important, because it means the search described cannot establish that relevant records did not exist, were never transferred, or were destroyed.



In particular, your response does not appear to address the other categories expressly identified in my request, including searches or recorded information relating to:



  *   Western Ground Rents Ltd;

  *   BP Pension Trust Ltd;

  *   BP Properties Ltd;

  *   Mountjoy Ltd;

  *   the proceedings in BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2;

  *   the 1982–1983 registration and associated government or administrative records;

  *   the 1980–1988 public campaign and governmental correspondence;

  *   the 1988 eviction and demolition;

  *   Cadw or central-government communications concerning the property;

  *   European Commission of Human Rights Application 14464/88;

  *   records concerning transfer, destruction or disposal of potentially relevant material; and

  *   HMC9/311 or related archival references.



These alternative lines of enquiry are intentional. The purpose is to establish whether relevant information can be identified through the government bodies, corporate entities, court proceedings, administrative processes and archival transfers associated with the property, rather than relying solely upon the modern name by which the property is known.



I am conducting corresponding enquiries with other repositories and public bodies. This is specifically intended to triangulate the documentary history where records may have been catalogued under a different creator, department, legal proceeding, estate, corporate body or administrative function.



I therefore ask that you do not treat the absence of a Discovery keyword hit as an answer to the substantive questions raised.



Please clarify:



  1.  Whether the searches undertaken were limited to the PRO and RW catalogue series and the four property/location search terms identified in your email.

BP Archive Team,

I am writing to enquire about records held within the BP corporate archive relating to the former Great House Farm / Ty Mawr property at Llandough, near Penarth, Glamorgan, South Wales.

I am conducting historical and legal research into the property, which was acquired by BP Pension Trust Ltd in December 1969 and subsequently administered by BP Properties Ltd. The property was the subject of extensive litigation, including BP Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, followed by the eviction of the occupying family in 1988 and demolition of the farmhouse later that year.

Research context

The central issue of my research is the identification of the individual parcels comprising the historic property.

The evidence currently being examined indicates that the historic complex may have comprised separately identifiable:

  *   a house-and-garden plot;
  *   a western agricultural/farm plot containing the barn, stables and courtyard; and
  *   an eastern cottages plot.

Later mapping and Land Registry records appear to have treated some of these areas as a combined property.

I am therefore particularly interested in establishing what BP itself understood the boundaries and constituent parcels of the property to be, and when any change or consolidation of those parcels occurred.

Records sought

I would be grateful if the BP Archive could search its holdings for records concerning:

  *   BP Properties Ltd;
  *   BP Pension Trust Ltd;
  *   British Petroleum and relevant predecessor/subsidiary property records;
  *   Great House Farm / Great House / Ty Mawr, Llandough;
  *   Llandough-juxta-Penarth / Cogan / Penarth;
  *   the Williams and Buckler families;
  *   possession proceedings and enforcement, particularly 1955, 1962 and 1974-1988;
  *   property acquisition, title investigation and disposal;
  *   conveyances, title deeds, abstracts of title and schedules of deeds;
  *   estate-management correspondence;
  *   property, site and boundary plans;
  *   Land Registry correspondence and registration, particularly 1982-1983.

The relevant period is approximately 1955-1988, with particular emphasis on 1962-1983.

Three priority categories

If relevant material survives, I would particularly like to identify the following, in this order:

1. The BP Properties Ltd / BP Pension Trust Ltd property file for Great House Farm / Ty Mawr, Llandough

In particular, any acquisition/title file containing the original property description, conveyances, title investigation, schedules of deeds, property plans, boundary plans or correspondence identifying exactly which land and buildings BP considered to form the property.

2. The legal/property file relating to the 1962 possession proceedings and subsequent enforcement/re-entry

In particular, any BP legal correspondence, instructions to solicitors, plans, property descriptions or internal documents identifying the land and buildings to which the possession order was understood to apply.

3. The 1982-1983 title/registration/consolidation file

In particular, correspondence, plans, conveyances, title investigation and Land Registry material concerning the registration or amalgamation of the relevant parcels, including any documentation showing how the house-and-garden, eastern cottages and western farm/barn/stables/courtyard areas were treated.

If these exact files do not survive, I would be very grateful for the nearest surviving files, alternative references or catalogue entries covering the same transactions.

Access

I would also appreciate advice on:

  *   whether the relevant records are available for public research;
  *   whether they can be viewed in person at the BP Archive at the University of Warwick;
  *   whether advance appointment or reader registration is required;
  *   whether particular records require advance retrieval;
  *   whether copies or digital reproductions can be ordered; and
  *   whether any relevant records are subject to closure or other access restrictions.

I am happy to provide further information, including the relevant court case reference, property names, dates and Land Registry title numbers, if this would assist the archivist in identifying the records.

Research purpose

I am particularly interested in contemporary BP documentation rather than later summaries, because the central research question is what BP itself understood the property's legal identity, boundaries and constituent parcels to be at the relevant dates.

Thank you very much for any assistance you can provide.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

FOI Team,

Thank you for your detailed response and for undertaking the additional
enquiries.

I appreciate the further information you have provided concerning the
searches undertaken. However, I would like to request an internal review
under the Freedom of Information Act 2000.

My concern is not simply that no objects have been identified. It is
whether the searches undertaken have fully addressed the scope of my
original request, particularly the documentary evidence concerning the
provenance, acquisition, transfer, ownership, identification and dispersal
of material originating from Great House Farm (Ty Mawr).

I would be grateful if the internal review could consider the following
points.

*1. Information identified concerning Great House Farm*

Your response states that the additional enquiries identified “some
information relating generally to Great House Farm and the surrounding
area”.

Please could you identify what categories of information this refers to
and, where it is not exempt, provide the relevant recorded information or
explain where it can be accessed?

This appears potentially relevant to the original request even if it does
not itself identify furniture or household objects.

*2. Scope of the archived electronic search*

You state that the Information Technology team reviewed “archived
electronic systems and records retained by the Museum”.

Please could the review clarify:

   - which archived systems were searched;
   - the approximate date ranges covered;
   - whether historical email or correspondence archives were searched;
   - whether legacy collections-management databases were searched;
   - whether databases or systems preceding the current CMS were searched;
   and
   - whether any archived systems were unavailable, incomplete or incapable
   of being searched.

*3. Correspondence and administrative records*

My original request expressly sought correspondence concerning the
identification, recovery, ownership or location of objects, as well as
correspondence with the Bute Estate, Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle and
other public authorities.

Your response refers generally to “associated collection documentation” and
“administrative records”, but does not make clear whether historical
correspondence files were specifically searched.

Please could the internal review establish whether searches were made of:

   - curator correspondence;
   - departmental correspondence files;
   - donor correspondence;
   - acquisition correspondence;
   - disposal correspondence;
   - loan correspondence;
   - provenance correspondence;
   - correspondence with Cardiff Council;
   - correspondence with Cardiff Castle;
   - correspondence with the Bute Estate;
   - correspondence with other museums or public authorities; and
   - any relevant institutional or external correspondence indexes.

*4. Search terms*

Thank you for identifying many of the search terms used.

Please could the internal review confirm whether the search also included
combinations and variants involving:

   - “Bute Estate”
   - “Bute”
   - “Cardiff Castle”
   - “Cardiff Council”
   - “Great House Farm”
   - “Ty Mawr”
   - “Great House”
   - “Llandough”
   - “Buckler”
   - “Williams”

   - “household effects”

   - “estate”
   - “dispersal”
   - “recovery”
   - “provenance”
   - “ownership”
   - “transfer”
   - “demolition”

I appreciate that historical records may not have been consistently
indexed, which is why I would be grateful for confirmation of the
methodology used.

*5. Transfer, disposal and destruction*

Your response states:

“We are also not aware of any relevant collection records relating to such
material having been transferred to another institution or destroyed.”

Please could the internal review clarify whether this conclusion is based
upon:

a. a search of transfer/accession-out records;

b. a review of retention and disposal records;

c. enquiries with relevant collections staff;

d. review of archival transfer documentation; or

e. institutional knowledge rather than a documentary search.

I am particularly interested in distinguishing between “no record exists”
and “no record was identified in the systems searched”.

*6. The original request concerning external institutions*

The original request was deliberately framed broadly because the question
concerns possible dispersal of the contents of a demolished historic
property.

It expressly included records concerning Cardiff Council, Cardiff Castle,
the Bute Estate, museums, Arts Council England, DCMS, RCEWA and other
public authorities.

I would therefore be grateful if the review could confirm whether records
of communications or transactions involving those bodies were searched
within Amgueddfa Cymru's records, rather than simply searching the Museum's

Thank you for your email.

Following receipt of your query, Amgueddfa Cymru undertook further enquiries to satisfy itself that no information had been overlooked when responding to your request.

These enquiries included a review of records held across the Museum's collections and a review of archived electronic systems and records by the Museum's Information Technology team. The review considered all collections management systems used by the Museum, including those most likely to contain information falling within the scope of your request.

For the History collections, searches were undertaken of the Collections Management System (CMS), accession files, donor indexes, location indexes and associated collection documentation. Searches were carried out using terms including "Great House Farm", "Ty Mawr", "Llandough", "Buckler" and "Bute". Additional consideration was given to acquisition records, provenance information and associated administrative records.

For the Art collections, searches were undertaken within the collections management system across description, comments, acquisition notes and place fields using the terms "Ty Mawr", "Great House Farm", "Great House", "Williams", "Buckler", "Llandough" and combinations of those terms. No additional paper archives relating to Great House Farm, Ty Mawr, Great House or Buckler were identified.

The Museum's Information Technology team also reviewed archived electronic systems and records retained by the Museum.

These enquiries identified some information relating generally to Great House Farm and the surrounding area. Thank you for your response.

I accept the distinction you draw between the Council's Corporate Concerns
and Complaints Policy and the separate statutory framework governing the
conduct of elected members. I am not seeking to use the corporate
complaints procedure as an appeal against historic planning, enforcement,
land or judicial decisions.

However, I do wish to clarify one important point concerning your decision
in your capacity as Monitoring Officer.

My complaint about Councillor George Carroll was not simply that the
Council should revisit historic decisions concerning Great House Farm. The
specific concern was his repeated failure to provide any substantive
response to correspondence sent to him in his capacity as the elected
councillor for Llandough, despite repeated approaches over a period of
approximately five months and despite the correspondence setting out
specific matters concerning his ward.

The chronology supplied with my complaint records correspondence on:

   - 16 February 2026;
   - 4 May 2026;
   - 7 June 2026;
   - 25 June 2026; and
   - 13 July 2026.

My complaint therefore concerned the conduct and handling of that
correspondence by an elected member, rather than asking the Monitoring
Officer to determine the underlying historical ownership or planning
dispute.

You state:

“Having reviewed the information you have provided, I have not identified
evidence which would indicate a breach of the Members Code of Conduct.”

I would therefore be grateful for clarification of the basis upon which
that conclusion was reached.

In particular, please confirm:

   1.

   *Which specific provisions of the Members' Code of Conduct were
   considered* in assessing my complaint.
   2.

   *Whether the complete correspondence chronology and the underlying
   emails and attachments were considered*, rather than merely my summary
   of them.
   3.

   *Whether Councillor Carroll was invited to provide an explanation or
   response* concerning the repeated absence of any substantive response to
   the correspondence.
   4.

   If so, whether his response was taken into account in reaching your
   conclusion.
   5.

   If not, please explain how the Monitoring Officer was able to determine
   that there was no evidence indicating a possible breach without obtaining
   the member's account of the conduct complained of.
   6.

   Please explain, in sufficient detail to enable me to understand the
   decision, *why the documented pattern of conduct was considered
   incapable of engaging any provision of the Members' Code of Conduct*.

I appreciate that failure to answer correspondence does not, by itself,
necessarily constitute a breach of the Code. I am not asserting that
proposition. My concern is that the Monitoring Officer appears to have
reached a definitive conclusion without identifying the relevant Code
provisions, the evidence considered, or the reasoning by which that
evidence was found insufficient.

I would also ask you to clarify whether you consider that the matter should
instead be referred to the *Public Services Ombudsman for Wales* for

I have considered it carefully. Unfortunately, it does not appear to answer
the FOI enquiry I submitted.

My request was deliberately framed more broadly than a simple catalogue
search for the words “Great House Farm”, “Ty Mawr”, “Llandough” or
“Cedfin”. I specifically asked The National Archives to identify recorded
information concerning the *existence, transfer, retention, destruction,
disposal or absence of records*, including records that might not be
catalogued under the property's later or local names.

Your response confirms only that you searched the PRO and RW series using:

“Great House Farm” OR “Ty Mawr” OR Llandough OR Cedfin

combined with “Glamorgan”, and that this produced no catalogue results.

You also correctly state that Discovery searches catalogue titles and
descriptions rather than the contents of records. That qualification is
important, because it means the search described cannot establish that
relevant records did not exist, were never transferred, or were destroyed.

In particular, your response does not appear to address the other
categories expressly identified in my request, including searches or
recorded information relating to:

   - Western Ground Rents Ltd;
   - BP Pension Trust Ltd;
   - BP Properties Ltd;
   - Mountjoy Ltd;
   - the proceedings in *BP Properties Ltd v Buckler* [1987] EWCA Civ 2;
   - the 1982–1983 registration and associated government or administrative
   records;
   - the 1980–1988 public campaign and governmental correspondence;
   - the 1988 eviction and demolition;
   - Cadw or central-government communications concerning the property;
   - European Commission of Human Rights Application 14464/88;
   - records concerning transfer, destruction or disposal of potentially
   relevant material; and
   - HMC9/311 or related archival references.

These alternative lines of enquiry are intentional. The purpose is to
establish whether relevant information can be identified through the
*government
bodies, corporate entities, court proceedings, administrative processes and
archival transfers associated with the property*, rather than relying
solely upon the modern name by which the property is known.

I am conducting corresponding enquiries with other repositories and public
bodies. This is specifically intended to triangulate the documentary
history where records may have been catalogued under a different creator,
department, legal proceeding, estate, corporate body or administrative
function.

I therefore ask that you do not treat the absence of a Discovery keyword
hit as an answer to the substantive questions raised.

Thank you for your further correspondence and for clarifying the purpose of your submission.

I understand the distinction you draw between seeking a review of the original 1988 decision and raising broader concerns about record-keeping, archival practice, and public accountability. However, the Committee's role is to scrutinise and hold the Welsh Government and associated public bodies to account in relation to policy, governance, and the use of public resources.

While I appreciate the broader administrative concerns you have identified, the issues raised in your correspondence arise from a specific historical case. The Committee does not have a role in reviewing or overseeing day-to-day operational decisions taken in individual cases. Accordingly, the Committee is unable to take forward the matters raised in your correspondence.

If you wish to pursue concerns regarding the management, retention or preservation of historical records, these matters are most appropriately raised with the relevant public authority or archival body responsible for those records. Similarly, concerns regarding the administration of a public body should be pursued through that body's complaints procedure and, where appropriate, with the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales.

Thank you for taking the time to write to the Committee and to set out your concerns in detail.

Yours sincerely,

From: Sion Buckler <[email redacted]>

Subject: Re: Acknowledgement from the Culture, Communications, Cymraeg and Sport Committee


Dear Ms James,

Thank you for your considered response.

I understand and accept that the Committee does not have a remit to adjudicate upon an individual dispute, determine whether a historical decision was lawful, or direct Cadw to reopen a particular case. My submission was deliberately framed so as not to ask the Committee to do any of those things.

I would, however, respectfully clarify one point, because I am concerned that the nature of the request may have been characterised more narrowly than intended.

The attached report expressly states that it is not a legal challenge, a forensic proof of wrongdoing, a complaint seeking adjudication, or a demand for reversal of the 1988 decision. Its stated purpose is historical record correction, archival explanation and administrative acknowledgement. In particular, it asks for an explanation of why almost none of the records concerning the 1988 assessment survive, whether that reflects the applicable record-retention arrangements, and whether the surviving independent evidence should be properly reflected in the permanent public record.

The central issue therefore extends beyond the merits of the individual 1988 listing assessment.

Cadw's 2026 FOI response confirms that an assessment took place, but that only two exterior photographs now survive; the assessment report, reasons for refusal, site notes, internal recommendations and consultation correspondence are no longer available. The report does not assert that this proves wrongdoing. Rather, it identifies a straightforward public-administration question: how can the adequacy and evidential basis of an irreversible public heritage decision be understood or scrutinised when the underlying administrative record no longer survives?

That seems potentially relevant to the Committee's stated function of scrutinising the administration and accountability of Welsh Government and associated public bodies, even if the Committee cannot itself determine whether the 1988 decision was correct.

I am therefore not asking the Committee to investigate the Buckler family's historical dispute with BP, adjudicate upon the 1988 decision, or direct Cadw to reverse anything. The specific administrative questions raised in the report are instead:

  1.  What record-retention arrangements applied to the 1988 assessment?
  2.  Why do the assessment report, reasons, site notes and consultation records no longer survive?
  3.  Were the records destroyed under an applicable retention policy or other authority, and were they considered for transfer to the appropriate archival institution?
  4.  Is the present position consistent with Welsh Government/Cadw expectations for the preservation of records concerning significant heritage decisions?
  5.  Are current arrangements sufficient to ensure that comparable heritage assessments, particularly where a building is under imminent threat of demolition, are properly documented and retained?

These are not questions that require the Committee to determine the rights of either party to the original dispute. They concern administrative practice, institutional record-keeping and the ability of the Senedd and the public to scrutinise decisions taken by public bodies. The report specifically asks Cadw to explain the archival position and review its current record-keeping practices for this reason.

I would therefore be grateful if the Committee could reconsider whether the broader administrative and accountability issue falls within its scrutiny function, even if the Committee cannot examine the underlying individual dispute.

If the Committee considers that it nevertheless cannot engage with the matter, I would appreciate clarification as to which Senedd or Welsh Government scrutiny, oversight, archival or complaints mechanism is considered appropriate for raising a documented concern about the absence of the administrative record of a historical Cadw decision and the implications this has for public accountability.

For completeness, I should also emphasise that the report itself deliberately recognises the limits of the surviving evidence. It does not claim that Cadw acted unlawfully or in bad faith, and it expressly acknowledges that the absence of the 1988 working papers means that the assessment cannot now be reconstructed definitively.

My objective is therefore quite limited: to ensure that the surviving evidence is preserved, that the archival gap is properly explained, and that the public record accurately distinguishes what is established from what can no longer be verified.

I hope that clarification assists, and I would be grateful if you could confirm whether the Committee is able to consider the matter from that wider public-administration and accountability perspective.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Dear Ms James,

Thank you for your considered response.

I understand and accept that the Committee does not have a remit to
adjudicate upon an individual dispute, determine whether a historical
decision was lawful, or direct Cadw to reopen a particular case. My
submission was deliberately framed so as not to ask the Committee to do any
of those things.

I would, however, respectfully clarify one point, because I am concerned
that the nature of the request may have been characterised more narrowly
than intended.

The attached report expressly states that it is *not a legal challenge, a
forensic proof of wrongdoing, a complaint seeking adjudication, or a demand
for reversal of the 1988 decision*. Its stated purpose is historical record
correction, archival explanation and administrative acknowledgement. In
particular, it asks for an explanation of why almost none of the records
concerning the 1988 assessment survive, whether that reflects the
applicable record-retention arrangements, and whether the surviving
independent evidence should be properly reflected in the permanent public
record.

The central issue therefore extends beyond the merits of the individual
1988 listing assessment.

Cadw's 2026 FOI response confirms that an assessment took place, but that
only two exterior photographs now survive; the assessment report, reasons
for refusal, site notes, internal recommendations and consultation
correspondence are no longer available. The report does not assert that
this proves wrongdoing. Rather, it identifies a straightforward
public-administration question: *how can the adequacy and evidential basis
of an irreversible public heritage decision be understood or scrutinised
when the underlying administrative record no longer survives?*

That seems potentially relevant to the Committee's stated function of
scrutinising the administration and accountability of Welsh Government and
associated public bodies, even if the Committee cannot itself determine
whether the 1988 decision was correct.

I am therefore not asking the Committee to investigate the Buckler family's
historical dispute with BP, adjudicate upon the 1988 decision, or direct
Cadw to reverse anything. The specific administrative questions raised in
the report are instead:

   1. What record-retention arrangements applied to the 1988 assessment?
   2. Why do the assessment report, reasons, site notes and consultation
   records no longer survive?
   3. Were the records destroyed under an applicable retention policy or
   other authority, and were they considered for transfer to the appropriate
   archival institution?
   4. Is the present position consistent with Welsh Government/Cadw
   expectations for the preservation of records concerning significant
   heritage decisions?
   5. Are current arrangements sufficient to ensure that comparable
   heritage assessments, particularly where a building is under imminent
   threat of demolition, are properly documented and retained?

These are not questions that require the Committee to determine the rights
of either party to the original dispute. They concern *administrative
practice, institutional record-keeping and the ability of the Senedd and
the public to scrutinise decisions taken by public bodies*. The report
specifically asks Cadw to explain the archival position and review its
current record-keeping practices for this reason.

I would therefore be grateful if the Committee could reconsider whether the
broader administrative and accountability issue falls within its scrutiny
function, even if the Committee cannot examine the underlying individual
dispute.

If the Committee considers that it nevertheless cannot engage with the
matter, I would appreciate clarification as to *which Senedd or Welsh
Government scrutiny, oversight, archival or complaints mechanism is
considered appropriate for raising a documented concern about the absence
of the administrative record of a historical Cadw decision and the
implications this has for public accountability*.

For completeness, I should also emphasise that the report itself
deliberately recognises the limits of the surviving evidence. It does not
claim that Cadw acted unlawfully or in bad faith, and it expressly
acknowledges that the absence of the 1988 working papers means that the
assessment cannot now be reconstructed definitively.

My objective is therefore quite limited: *to ensure that the surviving
evidence is preserved, that the archival gap is properly explained, and
that the public record accurately distinguishes what is established from
what can no longer be verified.*

I hope that clarification assists, and I would be grateful if you could
confirm whether the Committee is able to consider the matter from that
wider public-administration and accountability perspective.

Kind regards,

Sion Buckler (Ret’d Sergeant)
Royal Signals Cyber & Electronic Warfare Professional and Life Member

Dear Sion,

For your question on the date range, I looked at all the files we hold, including before and after the 1897 date. Our records go back to the 17th century and are up to the 21st century. So the dates you mentioned were checked.

2. Catalogue results which were considered unrelated. Would it be possible to provide the catalogue reference numbers and descriptions of those records, even where you consider them unrelated, together with the reason they were excluded?

It would be a very large list of reference numbers to send you, but you can search those key words on the online catalogue here: https://catalogue.postalmuseum.org/

3. Scope of the catalogue. Could you confirm whether this means that all existing Postal Museum archival holdings, including uncatalogued or incompletely catalogued material, are represented in the system searched, or whether there are categories of physical material which may not yet be represented?

For what you will find on the online catalogue: you will only find catalogued items. It includes the ones held at BT Archives. You can tell the difference on where the items are held by looking at the 'Held at' line. Here is an example (unrelated to your area of interest):

[cid:image006.png@01DD25AF.B869F840]

On my system of archival catalogue: we can search catalogued and uncatalogued items. I also searched the uncatalogued items for your keywords, but only unrelated records came up. In addition to that, most uncatalogued items are records which are less than 20 years old. Any file from c.late 1890s or 1900s is already catalogued so you can't miss them.

4. Restricted, closed or unprocessed material. Were any records identified which could potentially relate to the subject but which were unavailable because they were restricted, closed, uncatalogued, unprocessed or otherwise inaccessible?

The only material that would have restricted access would be records that hold individuals' private information. But considering all the people concerned were alive during the late 1800s and early 1900s, it's very unlikely anyone would still be alive and have any personal information that would still be up-to-date. The other type of records that are restricted are some philatelic items, which don't concern your research.

5. Records transferred to BT Archives. You explained that relevant telecommunications material appearing in the catalogue is held at BT Archives. Could you confirm whether the Postal Museum retains any transfer records, accession records, finding aids or other information identifying the particular GPO/Telegraph/Engineering records which were transferred to BT Archives? If there are catalogue references which would help BT Archives locate the underlying material, I would be very grateful for those.

We don't have any transfer records any longer, it's been too long ago since the records were transferred to BT Archives. But you can easily find out which items are held at BT Archives when searching our online catalogue. See above the screenshot. Using the Finding Number mentioned on one of our online catalogue entries, you should be able to trace the item by contacting BT Archives directly. They are the only ones who have the most up-to-date information about the archival items that were transferred to them.

6. The Williams connection

I'm afraid that we don't hold any record that aren't about postal employees. So we wouldn't be able to find anything about this individual in our records. If there is any record of him in the records held at BT Archives, it's not mentioned in any of the file's descriptions.

7. Preparatory and follow-up records

Concerning all the terms you listed, the relevant records would be kept at BT Archives, so I can't know more about it.

We have some books about Marconi in our reference library, but they are books destined to a general audience and you could find those books in most libraries. It's likely you are already familiar with the titles! Here is the list of books we hold, Online catalogue search 'Marconi lib*'<https://catalogue.postalmuseum.org/collections/search?s=marconi+lib*&qa%5Bkeyword_reference_type%5D=0&qa%5Bpartner%5D=&qa%5Bidentifier%5D=&qa%5Bdate_from%5D=&qa%5Bdate_to%5D=&qa%5Btitle%5D=&qa%5Bperson%5D=&qa%5Bplace%5D=&qa%5Bsubject%5D=&qa%5Bformat%5D=&cbpt=0&cbav=2&cbadvsearchquery=>

I hope those answers will help you in your future research.

Best regards,

Mathilde

Mathilde,

Thank you for clarifying the search methodology. Your explanation is helpful, particularly the distinction between records appearing in the Postal Museum catalogue and records physically held at BT Archives.

Before I proceed to BT Archives, I would like to make sure I understand the limits of the search correctly and avoid unnecessarily duplicating it.

There are a few further points which I would be grateful if you could clarify.

1. Date range

Was the search for the various names and locations conducted across the surrounding period, or was material effectively assessed only against the 1897 demonstration?

Could you confirm whether 1895-1900, including 1896, 1898, 1899 and 1900, was searched?

This is important because I am investigating not only the demonstration itself but also possible preparations beforehand and correspondence or reports afterwards.

2. Catalogue results which were considered unrelated

You mentioned that some results appeared for terms including Penarth, wireless demonstrations, GPO Telegraph Department, Engineering Department and Williams, but that they were considered unrelated after examination of their catalogue descriptions.

Would it be possible to provide the catalogue reference numbers and descriptions of those records, even where you consider them unrelated, together with the reason they were excluded?

I would prefer to examine those references myself rather than inadvertently overlooking something that may become relevant when considered alongside other records.

3. Scope of the catalogue

You have explained that the physical archives were not separately checked because the information is recorded on the archival cataloguing system.

Could you confirm whether this means that all existing Postal Museum archival holdings, including uncatalogued or incompletely catalogued material, are represented in the system searched, or whether there are categories of physical material which may not yet be represented?

4. Restricted, closed or unprocessed material

Were any records identified which could potentially relate to the subject but which were unavailable because they were restricted, closed, uncatalogued, unprocessed or otherwise inaccessible?

If so, I would be grateful for the relevant reference numbers and any applicable access restrictions.

5. Records transferred to BT Archives

You explained that relevant telecommunications material appearing in the catalogue is held at BT Archives.

Could you confirm whether the Postal Museum retains any transfer records, accession records, finding aids or other information identifying the particular GPO/Telegraph/Engineering records which were transferred to BT Archives?

If there are catalogue references which would help BT Archives locate the underlying material, I would be very grateful for those.

6. The Williams connection

The purpose of the search for Williams is not to establish that Mr Williams was a Post Office employee.

The family tradition concerns a local Mr Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough near Penarth, who may have assisted Marconi locally. Consequently, a relevant record might describe him as a local resident, landowner, farmer, host, assistant, carrier, messenger, proprietor or other private individual rather than as Post Office personnel.

Could you therefore confirm whether the search for Williams included references of this kind, rather than only Post Office employees or personnel records?

Similarly, were variants such as Mr Williams, W. Williams, William Williams and Williams considered?

7. Preparatory and follow-up records

Could the search also be considered in terms of records concerning:

  *   preparations for the South Wales experiments;
  *   arrangements made with local residents or property owners;
  *   visits to or use of private premises;
  *   transport or movement of equipment;
  *   correspondence immediately before or after the experiments;
  *   follow-up reports;
  *   subsequent demonstrations or experiments in the area;
  *   photographs, plans, maps or other material which might identify locations or participants.

I appreciate that you may ultimately conclude that none of these are held by the Postal Museum. I am simply trying to establish precisely what evidence has and has not survived, and where the relevant archival trail now leads.

Finally, if the Postal Museum has any contemporary publications, newspaper-cutting collections, photographs, finding aids or other material concerning the South Wales Marconi experiments, even where they do not specifically mention Great House Farm or Mr Williams, I would be grateful for those references as well.

Thank you again for your assistance. Your clarification has helped considerably in narrowing the search, and I appreciate your taking the time to establish exactly what the Postal Museum catalogue can and cannot tell me.

Kind regards,

information relating to criminal proceedings involving *William Beverly
("Billy") Buckler* arising from events connected with the eviction and
demolition of *Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan*,

individual case files.

texts.gm-19fc40e3ff740538:
Dear Dr. Driver,

I hope this message finds you well. I wanted first to offer my sincere
congratulations to you and the RCAHMW team on your recent aerial
discoveries. There is something almost magical about the way a sustained
spell of dry, sunny weather can strip back the concealment of centuries —
revealing sites of profound historical importance that grass and topsoil
have kept hidden from view for generations. It is a powerful reminder of
how much of our past lies just beneath the surface, waiting for the right
conditions to bring it back into the light.

I write to you, however, about a site whose concealment has not been
botanical, but bureaucratic and procedural. My family’s history — that of
Great House Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan — has been covered
up not by grass, but by what I can only describe, with careful precision,
as a major scandal of documentary disappearance, procedural irregularity,
and the systematic obscuring of a separate legal title.

The farm, which stood beside St Dochdwy’s Church from at least the 13th
century (and possibly as early as 1215), was home to the Williams family
from 1667 and later the Buckler line. In 1876, the Bute Estate severed 33
acres for the Llandough Limeworks. Family testimony, supported by estate
records, indicates that following this severance, the farmhouse, garden and
curtilage may have been treated as a separate legal parcel — a freehold
distinct from the surrounding agricultural leasehold. Yet this distinction,
if it existed, was progressively obscured through decades of litigation,
missing title deeds, and what appears to have been a conflation of two
distinct legal interests.

By the time of the 1987 Court of Appeal decision in BP Properties Ltd v
Buckler [1987] EWCA Civ 2, the question of historical title had never been
judicially determined. The court ruled on possession and the effect of a
1974 unilateral licence on adverse possession; it did not rule on whether
the Williams family held a separate freehold to the farmhouse plot. The
original Land Registry first-registration bundle (WA231076 / WA240304)
remains inaccessible following an FOI refusal. The 1971 Ordnance Survey
records have not been examined for descriptor shifts. And the 1667
transaction deed — a 999-year lease, effectively a virtual freehold — has
never been located.

The farm was demolished in December 1988. A 1994 rescue excavation by
Cotswold Archaeological Trust revealed 1,026 early-medieval inhumation
burials — the largest such population yet recovered from Wales — yet the
demolition proceeded without archaeological condition. The RCAHMW’s own
1974 floor plan (ST 16817331, H.W. Thomas) documented late 17th–19th
century features shortly before the final litigation. LiDAR data now show
anomalous features near the former site that may indicate a far larger
Roman landscape than previously understood.

What I am asking, Dr. Driver, is whether the RCAHMW — with its unique
statutory role in recording and protecting the historic environment of
Wales — might look again at this site, not with a drone or an aerial
camera, but with the same forensic attention to buried evidence that your
team applies to cropmarks. The grass that covers your aerial sites is
honest; it can be burned away by a hot summer. The concealment surrounding
Great House Farm is of a different order entirely — it lies in missing
documents, inaccessible registries, and a litigation record that addressed
possession while never determining title.

I would welcome the opportunity to share the full reconstructed chronology
(Version 7.0) with you, and to discuss whether RCAHMW records, surveys, or
cartographic archives might hold the key to uncovering what was truly lost
at Llandough.

With warm regards and renewed congratulations on your aerial survey
successes,

Hywel ap Buckler

On behalf of the Restored House of Williams / Buckler Family Estate

Great House, Manor of Llandough, Cardiff

helpful, particularly the distinction between records appearing in the
Postal Museum catalogue and records physically held at BT Archives.

Before I proceed to BT Archives, I would like to make sure I understand the

clarify.

*1. Date range*

Was the search for the various names and locations conducted across the
surrounding period, or was material effectively assessed only against the
1897 demonstration?

Could you confirm whether *1895–1900*, including 1896, 1898, 1899 and 1900,

This is important because I am investigating not only the demonstration
itself but also possible preparations beforehand and correspondence or
reports afterwards.

*2. Catalogue results which were considered unrelated*

You mentioned that some results appeared for terms including Penarth,
wireless demonstrations, GPO Telegraph Department, Engineering Department
and Williams, but that they were considered unrelated after examination of
their catalogue descriptions.

Would it be possible to provide the *catalogue reference numbers and
descriptions of those records*, even where you consider them unrelated,
together with the reason they were excluded?

I would prefer to examine those references myself rather than inadvertently
overlooking something that may become relevant when considered alongside
other records.

*3. Scope of the catalogue*

You have explained that the physical archives were not separately checked
because the information is recorded on the archival cataloguing system.

Could you confirm whether this means that *all existing Postal Museum
archival holdings, including uncatalogued or incompletely catalogued
material, are represented in the system searched*, or whether there are
categories of physical material which may not yet be represented?

*4. Restricted, closed or unprocessed material*

Were any records identified which could potentially relate to the subject
but which were unavailable because they were restricted, closed,
uncatalogued, unprocessed or otherwise inaccessible?

applicable access restrictions.

catalogue is held at BT Archives.

particular GPO/Telegraph/Engineering records which were transferred to BT

Dear Sion,

I searched our archive's catalogued, for all catalogued and uncatalogued items, using the following keywords:

  *   Great House Farm
  *   Llandough
  *   Lavernock
Result: no item is held in our archives using these words in the description.

  *   Penarth
  *   wireless demonstrations
  *   GPO Telegraph Department
  *   Engineering Department
  *   Williams / Mr Williams
Result: Some items held in our archives came up with those keywords, but when reading the description field on our catalogue, they turned out to be unrelated to the 1897 wireless telegraphy demonstration. Most were dated to before or after 1897. Many came up on our online catalogue, but they are held at BT Archives, therefore, we won't have any more information. This is what I meant by 'nothing relevant came up' - despite corresponding keyword, the dates or the content aren't related to your enquiry.
The physical archives were not checked as all information on our files are recorded on our archival cataloguing system, which is what I used to search information and keyword. You can search our online catalogue here: https://catalogue.postalmuseum.org/

I hope this helps,

letter.

could not previously be asked with precision.

been lodged with the first registration applications. That document does
not appear as a separate item in the schedule you have provided. Could you
please confirm whether:

the 1971 abstract of title survives as a separate document;

it forms part of one of the listed items (and if so, which); or

it is no longer held.

first registration application in which the applicant’s solicitors stated
they were “not aware of any question or doubt affecting the title”. Your
schedule identifies the surviving first-registration application as Form 1E
(item 13 for WA231076). Could you please confirm whether that certificate
forms part of the surviving Form 1E, and if not, identify the surviving
document in which it appears.

actually contained in the surviving first-registration records you have
listed.

first-registration application, the A13/DL list of documents lodged, the
correspondence with Linklaters & Paines, any related applications, and any
surviving examiner’s notes, file notes, memoranda or internal
correspondence — contain any reference to:

Mary Williams (also known as Mrs Buckler);

Fred Buckler;

Ty Mawr;

Great House Farm;

any assertion by another person that they owned, occupied, or claimed an
interest in the land;

any ownership dispute, possession proceedings, litigation, or competing
claim affecting the land;

any issue, doubt, objection, caution, competing interest, or other matter
affecting title.

first-registration records contain any indication that another party
asserted ownership of, or claimed an interest in, the land before first

in your letter of 30 July 2026.

Dear Mr Buckler

Many thanks for your email, apologies for the delay in responding I have been on annual leave. To answer your queries I must refer you back to my previous emails of the 10th 3rd and 2nd July.

I appreciate your concerns and desires to find the information. However, I can confirm that all records were checked for the information you requested and we hold no further information or a record of the destruction. Cadw’s inspector advised, based on his experience, that he understood the practice was to either transfer records to the RCAHMW or destroy them under the Public Records Act 1958. We have no record of any transfer lists, accession records, archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records relating to Great House Farm were ever transferred to the RCAHMW.  The photograph provides the only documentary evidence that Great House Farm was visited by Cadw and did not meet the criteria as it was not included on the list.

To be clear, we do not have any further information which would help with your search for the relevant information. If you remain dissatisfied with this response you have the right to complain to the Information Commissioner. The Information Commissioner can be contacted at:

Information Commissioner’s Office,

Wycliffe House,

Water Lane,

Wilmslow,

Cheshire,
[postcode redacted].

Kind Regards

Amy

Ms Longford,

Before responding to my earlier email, please may I add the following to my enquiry, even if you require addition time to respond due to this addition to my enquiry;

In addition to my email of 2 July, there are a small number of further points which I would be grateful if you could address as they arise directly from comparing the original response with the internal review.

The original response of 11 June 2026 stated:

"Any other associated records would have been either transferred to the Royal Commission on the Ancient & Historical Monuments of Wales for permanent preservation, or destroyed under the Public Record Act 1958."

However, the internal review of 2 July 2026 states instead that:

"There is also no evidence that any relevant files have been transferred to the RCAHMW."

and

"It is possible that the file was destroyed before it was ever updated on our electronic filing system."

These appear to be materially different positions.

Accordingly, I would be grateful if you could clarify the following:

  1.  What evidence supported the original statement that any associated records would have been transferred to the RCAHMW or destroyed under the Public Records Act 1958?
  2.  Following the internal review, does Welsh Government now accept that there is no evidence that any relevant records were transferred to the RCAHMW?
  3.  Does Welsh Government hold any transfer lists, accession records, archive schedules or other documentation recording whether records relating to Great House Farm were ever transferred to the RCAHMW?
  4.  If no such documentation exists, on what evidential basis was the original statement regarding transfer to the RCAHMW made?
  5.  Likewise, if there is no destruction register, disposal log or audit trail relating to the relevant file, on what evidential basis has destruction been suggested?

Finally, the original response stated as fact that Great House Farm was visited by Cadw inspectors and did not meet the statutory listing criteria. The internal review, however, confirms that no assessment, report or case file has been located.

Could you therefore identify the documentary evidence upon which that conclusion was based, or alternatively confirm whether the statement in the original response was an inference drawn from the existence of the two photographs rather than from any surviving assessment records.

These points are intended simply to clarify the historical record and to reconcile what appear to be two materially different explanations contained within the original response and the internal review.

Thank you again for your assistance, and I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,



Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sergenant)

Thank you for your letter of 2 July 2026 responding to the internal review of my Freedom of Information request (ATISN 27021) concerning Great House Farm, Llandough.

However, having considered both the original response of 11 June 2026 and the outcome of the internal review, I would be be grateful if you could clarify a number of points which appear to remain unresolved.

The original response stated that Great House Farm was visited and assessed by Cadw inspectors and that the building did not satisfy the statutory listing criteria.

The internal review now confirms that no assessment, report or case file relating to that decision has been located and further states that any relevant file may have been destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please therefore identify the documentary basis upon which the original response concluded that the property was assessed and found not to meet the listing criteria.

Specifically:

  *   Is that conclusion derived from a surviving record?
  *   If so, please identify that record.
  *   If not, please explain how that conclusion was reached.

2. The inspection of 29 July 1988

The original disclosure included two photographs dated 29 July 1988.

Please confirm:

  *   whether those photographs were taken as part of a formal listing inspection;
  *   whether they formed part of a wider inspection file;
  *   whether any inspection notes, recommendation forms, field notebooks, photographic registers or other associated records were created; and
  *   if such records once existed, whether they are now believed to have been destroyed.

3. Basis for the statement that records may have been destroyed

The review states that it is possible documentation dating from around 1988 was destroyed before being entered onto the electronic records system.

Please clarify whether that statement is based upon:

  *   documentary evidence relating specifically to Great House Farm;
  *   records management documentation such as retention schedules, destruction registers or disposal logs; or
  *   a general understanding of historic records management practices.

If no destruction records exist for the relevant file series, please confirm this.

4. Scope of the searches

Please confirm whether searches extended beyond the registered listing files to include, where appropriate:

  *   ministerial correspondence;
  *   senior officials' correspondence;
  *   legal files;
  *   inspector's working papers;
  *   site visit records;
  *   archaeological or conservation files;
  *   policy records; and
  *   correspondence with external organisations, including the Vale of Glamorgan Council, the former Welsh Office and other heritage bodies.

If any of these categories were not searched, I would be grateful if you could identify which.

5. Welsh Government's position

Finally, I would be appreciate clarification of the Welsh Government's position regarding Great House Farm.

Does the Welsh Government's position now amount to one of the following:

  *   that Great House Farm was never considered for statutory protection;
  *   that it was considered, but the records no longer survive; or
  *   that it is no longer possible to determine whether consideration took place because the relevant records are unavailable?

If none of those accurately reflects your position, I would be grateful if you could explain what the Welsh Government's position is.

These questions arise directly from the original response and the internal review and are intended to clarify the historical record rather than seek the creation of new information.

I look forward to your response.

Yours sincerely,

Sion Buckler

Dear Sion,

Thank you for your enquiry. I will do my best to check if we have surviving records of this demonstration, although most of the records about telecommunications were transferred to BT Archives so they might have more information than us: https://www.bt.com/about/bt/our-history/bt-archives

  *   Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth, Cardiff (not Great House Farm, Llandough near Cowbridge)
I couldn't find any record mentioning Great House Farm, Llandough. For Penarth, there were some results but they were all dated much later than the demonstration. We have many records on Cardiff, which you can find on our online catalogue Here, but nothing relevant seemed to have come up.

  *   Llandough, Penarth, Lavernock and the surrounding wireless demonstration sites.
Nothing came up for Lavernock either, the locations are too precise for this type of records to have reached our archives. I searched for 'wireless demonstration' and POST 88 Series titled 'Post Office: Wireless Telegraphy and Telephony' mentions such events, but all the files are kept in BT Archives.

  *   Guglielmo Marconi's 1897 demonstrations.
Almost all the files related to Marconi are held in BT Archives.

  *   GPO Telegraph or Engineering Department records concerning these demonstrations.
See above.

  *   Correspondence, reports, notebooks, diaries, staff lists, expense claims, photographs or plans relating to engineers or officials present.
See above.

  *   Any references to Mr Williams of Great House Farm, Llandough, who family history suggests assisted Marconi before, during or after his stay at the property.
I couldn't find any specific file about a Mr William from Great House Farm, but the main records we have that are useful for family history research are the Appointment Books, and the pension and gratuity records. We also have Establishment Books and staff magazines that can be helpful too. You can find more information about what we hold here:  https://www.postalmuseum.org/collections/the-archive/family-history/  Please bear in mind that most villages, small towns, hamlets, etc. such as Llandough had business that ran a postal service, and these people were not directly employed by the Post Office, therefore, we won't have any information. If Mr Williams had another business, he was likely not employed by the Post Office. A local archive might hold newspaper cuttings or other information about this person: https://glamarchives.gov.uk/
You are welcome to visit our archives, but I believe most of the records and information you are looking for will be held at BT Archives. You can contact them directly to organise an appointment.

I hope this helps,

Best regards,

Mathilde

If another archive holds any of these records, I would be grateful if you could advise where I should direct my enquiry.

Mr Williams of Great House Farm was my great grandad. I am trying to ascertain if the Mr Williams post office worker, mentioned helping Marconi in the article, was the same man as my great grandfather. I am also looking for any more connections between my family, my former home and Marconi and the radio experiments at lavernock point. Which I understand were already underway before Marconi arrived to South Wales.

Thank you for your time and assistance. I look forward to your response.

Kind regards,



Sion Buckler (Ret'd Sgt)

I am requesting your urgent assistance and referral to the appropriate
oversight bodies regarding serious and ongoing difficulties obtaining
historic records required for my family’s claim concerning Great House Farm
(Tŷ Mawr), Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan.

I want to be clear that I am not asking you to determine the underlying
ownership dispute. That is a matter for legal adjudication. I am requesting
assistance to ensure that the documentary evidence required for a fair
legal determination is identified, preserved and made available.

referral through my Member of Parliament. Who doesn't reply. The Llandough
councillor doesn't reply. I follow up monthly and nothing. The council
clerk for Llandough initially refused to cooperate then retired. CADW
initially lied to me too.

After more than a year of attempting to obtain records through Freedom of
Information requests, Environmental Information Regulations requests,
archive enquiries and correspondence with relevant bodies, I have
encountered repeated difficulties which are preventing proper assessment of
my family’s claim. South Wales Police say they don't hold records yet they
were reported by ITV and other news outlets as being heavily involved in
the dispossession of our land and home in 1988. Before our 80p year old
home was abruptly demolished and our land and home since 1667 seized .
Along with all our furniture, artwork etc, originally from Cardiff castle.
Property and reference information

*Great House Farm / Tŷ Mawr*
Llandough, Vale of Glamorgan

Relevant Land Registry titles:

   - WA231076
   - WA240304

Historic Ordnance Survey references:

   - 38-1-334

vs Buckler 1987 was dismissed and his ECHR rejected and then planning
permission approved.

I'm a former military cyber and electronic warfare professional, in
addition to being my dads son, nans grandson and child from this
dispossession in 1988. Which included what maybe SAS undercover as BP
Bailiffs. Both ripping me from my birthland and demolishing it in front of
us. Along with 2 toddlers siblings and my pregnant mum, who's shoulder they
dislocated while she served them an injuction to prevent them demolishing
or stealing our property.

Fraud unravels all. And the limitation is from discovery not occurance of

land registry we challenged their claim with our claim to the land.

All records relating to the demolition of Great House Farm in December

Ms Daniel,

Thank you for your response dated 20 July 2026 regarding FOI/2026/09 and
for identifying the catalogue references relating to Ty Mawr/Llandough
within the Bute Estate collections.

I would like to request an internal review, as I believe the response may
have interpreted the scope of my request too narrowly.

My request was for:

"All recorded information held concerning furniture, furnishings, antiques,
fixtures, heirlooms and other movable property originating from Great House
Farm (Ty Mawr), Llandough, including any and all items received from Bute
Estate, Cardiff Castle, Cardiff Council."

I appreciate that the National Library of Wales does not collect furniture
as a category of object and therefore may not hold the physical items
themselves. However, my request was not limited to physical objects or
acquisition files. It sought *all recorded information* relating to such
items.

This could include, for example:

   - inventories;
   - valuations;
   - estate correspondence;
   - fixture schedules;
   - probate references;
   - sale catalogues;
   - photographs;
   - tenancy records;
   - references within Bute Estate papers;
   - records of transfer, removal or disposal.

The response confirms that NLW holds significant Bute Estate material
relating to Ty Mawr, including maps, leases and deeds. However, it does not
clarify whether those wider collections were searched for references to the
farmhouse contents, fixtures, or related estate administration records.

Could the internal review please clarify:

   1.

   What collections and record series were searched in responding to this
   request?
   2.

   Were searches undertaken beyond acquisition files, including within Bute
   Estate papers and related archival collections?
   3.

   Were terms such as:


   - Great House Farm;
   - Ty Mawr;
   - Llandough;
   - fixtures;
   - inventory;
   - valuation;
   - contents;
   - furnishings;
   - sale;
   - transfer;

used as part of the search?

   4. If no relevant records are held, could you please confirm the
   searches undertaken and the basis for that conclusion?

The reason this distinction matters is that my wider research concerns the
documentary history of the farmhouse and garden plot following changes
affecting Ty Mawr/Llandough after the 19th century. Records relating to
fixtures, valuations, inventories or estate administration may provide

Our remit covers complaints where someone believes they've been treated unfairly or received poor service from NHS organisations or from UK government departments and their associated public organisations.

If the complaint involves public health services in Wales, this will usually fall under the remit of the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales: https://www.ombudsman.wales/

If your concerns are primarily about judicial decisions and potential violations of his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). As the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) does not have the remit to investigate judicial decisions, you could consider the following options:

  1.  Judicial Reviews and Appeals:
You will need to seek independent legal advice about the possibility of appealing the decisions or applying for a judicial review. Legal professionals can guide you on the feasibility of further legal action.
  2.  European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR):
If you believe your rights under the ECHR have been violated, you may wish to bring his case to the ECtHR. You will need to review the criteria for applying to the ECtHR at the court’s official website: https://www.echr.coe.int/.
  3.  Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC):
The EHRC provides guidance and support concerning human rights and discrimination issues in England, Scotland, and Wales. You can contact them for information or assistance: https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/en.
  4.  Citizens Advice:
For free, impartial advice, you could approach Citizens Advice, which may guide you on your next steps, including accessing pro bono legal services: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/.
I hope you find this information useful.

*Editor / Investigations Desk*

Dear Editor,

I am writing to ask your investigations team to examine what I believe is a
significant public-interest story involving one of the most influential
adverse possession cases in modern English and Welsh property law: *BP
Properties Ltd v Buckler [1987] 2 EGLR 168* (also reported as *(1988) 55 P
& CR 337*).

This Court of Appeal decision continues to be cited in legal textbooks and
case law. It established that a unilateral letter from the paper title
owner granting a rent-free licence could prevent adverse possession, even
where the occupier had not expressly accepted it. The case has shaped
property law for almost forty years.

My concern is not simply with the legal judgment itself.

It is with what surrounded it.

For several years I have been investigating the history of my family's
occupation of *Great House Farm, Llandough, near Penarth*, and the events
leading to the litigation. Through hundreds of Freedom of Information
requests, archive searches, Land Registry enquiries, historical research
and correspondence with public authorities, I have uncovered what I believe
are serious inconsistencies, missing records and evidence of institutional
concealment that deserve independent scrutiny.

Among the matters that I believe warrant investigation are:

   - Whether material evidence relating to the occupation and ownership of
   Great House Farm was withheld or never presented.
   - The circumstances surrounding the registration of title by BP
   interests in 1982 despite the long-running dispute.
   - Missing or unexplained historical records across multiple public
   bodies.
   - Whether public authorities have failed to preserve records concerning
   a nationally significant legal case.
   - Whether subsequent institutions have frustrated attempts to obtain
   records through Freedom of Information legislation.
   - The wider implications if a leading legal precedent was built upon an
   incomplete or inaccurate factual record.

My investigation has revealed repeated examples of authorities either
claiming records do not exist, directing me elsewhere, or providing
documents unrelated to the requests made. Numerous archives acknowledge
gaps where relevant material would ordinarily be expected.

I have also experienced what I believe to be persistent obstruction. My
elected representatives have failed to engage despite repeated requests.
Complaints have been redirected without investigation. During my enquiries,
a court employee whom I challenged over contradictory information left
their position shortly afterwards. While I cannot infer the reason for that
departure, the wider pattern has made it exceptionally difficult to
establish an accurate historical record.

This story extends far beyond a private family dispute.

It concerns:

   - whether powerful institutions have been properly held accountable;
   - preservation of public records;
   - transparency within government;
   - the development of UK property law;
   - the treatment of ordinary families in litigation against major
   corporations;
   - and whether historical injustices can remain effectively hidden
   because records disappear over time.

The human story is equally compelling.

My family lived through decades of litigation, uncertainty and eventual
displacement. The farmhouse was ultimately demolished, ending centuries of
family association with the property. Much of my family—particularly the
women—have lived with the consequences for generations and remain reluctant
to speak publicly because of the trauma. My brother and I are now
attempting to reconstruct the historical record before more evidence
disappears.

The property itself has remarkable historical significance. Great House
Farm has connections with the historic Bute Estate, archaeological
discoveries including Roman remains, and local accounts associated with the
pioneering wireless experiments at Lavernock Point during the Marconi era.
Yet the legal battle that made national case law has largely eclipsed that
wider history.

This investigation is supported by:

   - extensive documentary evidence;
   - Land Registry correspondence;
   - Freedom of Information responses from multiple public authorities;
   - archive references from national and local repositories;
   - court documents;
   - historical maps;
   - newspaper reports;
   - and a detailed chronology spanning more than a century.

I have also recorded my testimony explaining the evidence, chronology and
impact on my family: https://youtu.be/XuArB_vYWWA?si=O7TL2i5ocU3vn5fG

I am prepared to provide your journalists with a fully indexed evidence
archive, original source documents, timelines, witness information where
available, and copies of all official correspondence.

I am *not* asking your newspaper to accept my conclusions without question.

I am asking you to investigate.

If my concerns are unfounded, they should be capable of being disproved
through proper scrutiny. If they are substantiated, they raise serious
questions about one of the UK's leading property law authorities,
institutional accountability, public record keeping and the treatment of an
ordinary family whose story has never properly been told.

This is not simply a historical dispute.

It is a story about how legal precedents are created, how power operates,
whether the historical record can be trusted, and whether ordinary citizens
can ever obtain accountability decades after the events in question.

I believe it is exactly the kind of investigation that serves the public
interest.

I would welcome the opportunity to speak with one of your investigative
journalists and provide unrestricted access to the evidence I have
assembled.

*Yours faithfully,*

*Sion Buckler*

Dear Sion Bucker

Thank you for your email with the subject heading ' complaint of maladministration - defective notice, enforcement process, and loss of opportunity (Great House Farm, Llandough).

Our remit covers complaints where someone believes they've been treated unfairly or received poor service from NHS organisations or from UK government departments and their associated public organisations.

If the complaint involves public health services in Wales, this will usually fall under the remit of the Public Services Ombudsman for Wales: https://www.ombudsman.wales/

Similarly, if the complaint is related to how a solicitor or legal professional has handled a case, it is likely to fall under the jurisdiction of the Legal Ombudsman: https://www.legalombudsman.org.uk/

If your complaint is about HMCTS then you will need to complete the full complaints process and provide us with the formal response with an MP's referral.  You can follow the link below for further information on the full complaint process:

https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/hm-courts-and-tribunals-service/about/complaints-procedure

If your concerns are primarily about judicial decisions and potential violations of his rights under the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). As the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) does not have the remit to investigate judicial decisions, you could consider the following options:

  1.  Judicial Reviews and Appeals:
You will need to seek independent legal advice about the possibility of appealing the decisions or applying for a judicial review. Legal professionals can guide you on the feasibility of further legal action.
  2.  European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR):
If you believe your rights under the ECHR have been violated, you may wish to bring his case to the ECtHR. You will need to review the criteria for applying to the ECtHR at the court's official website: https://www.echr.coe.int/.
  3.  Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC):
The EHRC provides guidance and support concerning human rights and discrimination issues in England, Scotland, and Wales. You can contact them for information or assistance: https://www.equalityhumanrights.com/en.
  4.  Citizens Advice:
For free, impartial advice, you could approach Citizens Advice, which may guide you on your next steps, including accessing pro bono legal services: https://www.citizensadvice.org.uk/.
I hope you find this information useful.

Yours Sincerely,


Anita Eastham
Intake Caseworker
Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman

E: [email redacted]<[email redacted]>
W: www.ombudsman.org.uk<http://www.ombudsman.org.uk/>
